newsitem.title: UK: OPEC's Rakad cautions against oil price complacency.
newsitem.headline: OPEC's Rakad cautions against oil price complacency.

text.p: Following are excerpts from the speech by OPEC President and acting UAE Oil Minister Rakad bin Salem bin Rakad to the 101st meeting of the OPEC conference in Vienna on Wednesday as reported by the OPECNA news agency, monitored in London:

Six months ago, we successfully completed the 100th meeting of the OPEC conference. We must now turn our attention towards the next series of meetings and the fresh set of challenges that await us. Some of these challenges will be more serious than others.

But, after three and a half decades of dedication and commitment to our member countries' collective interests - among which is the achievement of sustainable order, stability and equity in the international oil market - we remain ever-confident of opec's ability to cope successfully with any future market situation.
As we begin the 101st meeting of the conference, we have the pleasure of welcoming both a new colleague and an old colleague to our ranks, as heads of their distinguished countries' delegations.

The new colleague is the minister of oil for Kuwait, his Excellency Issa Mohammed al-Mazidi; the old colleague is the former minister of oil for Iraq, his Excellency Osama al-Hiti, now advisor at the presidential office, who is sitting in for his excellency Dr Amer Mohammed Rasheed, Iraq's oil minister. We look forward to their valuable contributions on the state of the oil market and the general welfare of our organization...

The events of the past six months in the international oil market have taken many people by surprise. After a long period of market weakness, we have begun to witness price levels last seen, in regular market conditions, more than a decade ago.

The weekly average basket price almost touched us $24 per barrel in october. This is well over 40 per cent higher than the average annual figures for each of the past three years. The general impression is that market fundamentals have been sturdier than many analysts had predicted.

The jump in prices that began in early September reflected fears within the industry that crude and product stocks, particularly heating oil, were unusually low, and might create a shortfall in the approaching northern hemisphere winter, especially if it turned out to be another severe one.
In addition, world oil demand has been higher and non-OPEC supply lower than predicted. The delay in the implementation of Iraq's food-for-oil deal, as well as uncertainties in the international poli

The higher oil prices have been accompanied by a strong dollar, notably with respect to the values of two of the world's leading currencies, the deutschmark and the yen. Together, the high prices and strong dollar have provided a welcome boost to our member countries' oil revenues.

Yet, in spite of the present improved conditions, we must guard against taking the situation for granted. As we are well aware, market fortunes can change radically and rapidly in a short space of time.

Oil's central role in the modern consumer- oriented society makes it highly vulnerable to non-economic influences, especially where they are of a political, strategic or purely self-interested nature. These are often seen in the decisions and actions of diverse powerful interests, sometimes far removed from the practical workings of the oil industry itself.

A notable example is the ongoing debate on global warming, and the resultant threat of the widespread implementation of unfair energy taxes, which would be highly damaging to our member countries' economies. Another is the longstanding call to reduce dependence on opec oil.
While I do not wish to dwell on such issues in this address, they nevertheless represent an important part of the background to our discussions.

OPEC, while recognising the diverse nature of legitimate interests among the parties within the market, seeks to consistently pursue a policy of co-operation and harmony. Decisions and actions should satisfy both short-term situations and longer-term fundamentals. If managed properly, these should not be in conflict with each other.

In essence, the issue is a simple one - to supply oil to those who need it, on mutually beneficial terms. Everything else should be secondary to this. We should ensure that our attention remains focused on our deep-rooted commitment to satisfy the collective, responsible interests of our member countries in the best manner possible. It is with this is mind that we should proceed with this meeting.
